e-3063.knowledge_point: Finding an Integral Expression For the Arc Length of a Curve
e-3063.problem:
Write down the integral that gives the arc length of the curve  $\mathbf f (t) = \langle 3 \sin t, \: 2\sin 2t \rangle$
from $t =\dfrac {3\pi} 2$  to $t = 2\pi.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14081725/assets/574a16e843a9c81e5fc9ddbbe2c0dc2c308ffcac4991bcbf48c7f45b4871c93b.png)
e-3063.worked_solution:
First, we find $\mathbf f'(t)$ and $\|\mathbf f'(t)\|\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)⟩ \\  & =⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩ \\ ‖{f}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(4\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9{cos}^{2}⁡t+16{cos}^{2}⁡2t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{a}^{b}‖{f}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }\sqrt{9{cos}^{2}⁡t+16{cos}^{2}⁡2t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

e-3064.knowledge_point: Computing the Arc Length of a Planar Curve
e-3064.problem:
Find the arc length of the curve $\mathbf g (t) = \langle 3 - 2 \sin 2t, \: 1 - 2\cos 2t \rangle$ from $t=\dfrac \pi 3$ to $\pi.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14081725/assets/29c97e5963d451cc389944ef113764b2d15998448e773a02bb98c062207c2860.png)
e-3064.worked_solution:
First, we find $\mathbf g'(t)$ and $\|\mathbf g'(t)\|\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-4\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡2t⟩ \\ ‖{g}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(-4\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)^{2}+(4\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16{cos}^{2}⁡2t+16{sin}^{2}⁡2t} \\  & =\sqrt{16} \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{a}^{b}‖{g}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi }4\,\text{d}t \\  & =4t\,{|}_{\pi /3}^{\pi } \\  & =4(\pi -\frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =\frac{8\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Arc length is ∫₋₁¹‖f′(t)‖ dt. Here f′(t)=⟨cos t−sin t,e^t,cos t+sin t⟩, so ‖f′(t)‖²=(cos t−sin t)²+e^(2t)+(cos t+sin t)²=e^(2t)+2. Thus option e is correct.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem: Which integral expression gives the arc length of the curve $f(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{e}^{t},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩$ from $t=-1$ to $t=1?$
after.worked_solution:
First, we find ${f}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{f}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{e}^{t},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\ ‖{f}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+({e}^{t})^{2}+{(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡t-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t+{e}^{2t}+{cos}^{2}⁡t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+2({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}‖{f}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+2}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1

Which integral expression gives the arc length of the curve f(t)=⟨cos⁡t+sin⁡t,et,sin⁡t−cos⁡t⟩ from t=−1 to t=1?

a
∫−112et+1dt
b
∫−11e2t+1dt
c
2∫−11et+2dt
d
2∫−112e2t+1dt
e
∫−11e2t+2dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we find f′(t) and ‖f′(t)‖: f′(t)=⟨ddt(cos⁡t+sin⁡t),ddt(et),ddt(sin⁡t−cos⁡t)⟩=⟨cos⁡t−sin⁡t,et,cos⁡t+sin⁡t⟩‖f′(t)‖=(cos⁡t−sin⁡t)2+(et)2+(cos⁡t+sin⁡t)2=cos2⁡t−2cos⁡tsin⁡t+sin2⁡t+e2t+cos2⁡t+2cos⁡tsin⁡t+sin2⁡t=e2t+2(cos2⁡t+sin2⁡t)=e2t+2

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is L=∫−11‖f′(t)‖dt=∫−11e2t+2dt.

content.knowledge_point: Finding an Integral Expression For the Arc Length of a Curve
content.problem: Which integral expression gives the arc length of the curve $f(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{e}^{t},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩$ from $t=-1$ to $t=1?$
content.worked_solution:
First, we find ${f}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{f}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{e}^{t},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\ ‖{f}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+({e}^{t})^{2}+{(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡t-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t+{e}^{2t}+{cos}^{2}⁡t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+2({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}‖{f}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+2}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

Which integral expression gives the arc length of the curve h(t)=cos⁡ti+sin⁡tj+tk from t=0 to t=2π?

a
∫02π2+sin2⁡tdt
b
∫02π2+cos2⁡tdt
c
∫0π3−sin2⁡tdt
d
∫02π2sin2⁡t+cos2⁡tdt
e
∫02π2dt
Submit

decision.explanation: The derivative is h′(t)=⟨−sin t,cos t,1⟩, whose magnitude is √(sin²t+cos²t+1)=√2. Integrating this speed from 0 to 2π gives option e.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14081725/assets/d42e9c6ed71f06c2dec273a91d3a4cfbdf5c58095be9370285d7987d38f7b5a6.png)

Which integral  expression gives the arc length of the curve $h(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+t\,k$ from  $t=0$ to $t=2\pi ?$
after.worked_solution:
First, we find ${h}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{h}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,k \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+1\,k \\ ‖{h}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t+1} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is:

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }‖{h}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

Which integral expression gives the arc length of the curve h(t)=cos⁡ti+sin⁡tj+tk from t=0 to t=2π?

a
∫02π2+sin2⁡tdt
b
∫02π2+cos2⁡tdt
c
∫0π3−sin2⁡tdt
d
∫02π2sin2⁡t+cos2⁡tdt
e
∫02π2dt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we find h′(t) and ‖h′(t)‖:

h′(t)=ddt(cos⁡t)i+ddt(sin⁡t)j+ddt(t)k=−sin⁡ti+cos⁡tj+1k‖h′(t)‖=(−sin⁡t)2+(cos⁡t)2+(1)2=sin2⁡t+cos2⁡t+1=2

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is: L=∫02π‖h′(t)‖dt=∫02π2dt

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms h′(t)=⟨−sin t,cos t,1⟩ and ‖h′(t)‖=√(sin²t+cos²t+1)=√2. Thus the arc length integral is option e. The incorrect feedback concerns the deliberately submitted option c.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14081725/assets/d42e9c6ed71f06c2dec273a91d3a4cfbdf5c58095be9370285d7987d38f7b5a6.png)

Which integral  expression gives the arc length of the curve $h(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+t\,k$ from  $t=0$ to $t=2\pi ?$
content.worked_solution:
First, we find ${h}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{h}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,k \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+1\,k \\ ‖{h}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t+1} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is:

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }‖{h}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

a
∫2516t6+9t4+9dt
b
∫2516t6+9t4dt
c

decision.explanation: r′(t)=⟨3t²,3,4t³⟩, so ‖r′(t)‖=√(9t⁴+9+16t⁶). Integrating this speed from 2 to 5 gives option a.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem: Which integral expression gives the arc length of the curve $r(t)={t}^{3}\,i+3t\,j+{t}^{4}\,k$ from  $t=2$ to $t=5?$
after.worked_solution:
First, we find ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{4})\,k \\  & =3{t}^{2}\,i+3\,j+4{t}^{3}\,k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(3{t}^{2})^{2}+(3)^{2}+(4{t}^{3})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9{t}^{4}+9+16{t}^{6}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is:

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{2}^{5}‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t={\int }_{2}^{5}\sqrt{16{t}^{6}+9{t}^{4}+9}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Which integral expression gives the arc length of the curve r(t)=t3i+3tj+t4k from t=2 to t=5?

a
∫2516t6+9t4+9dt
b
∫2516t6+9t4dt
c
∫0516t6+9dt
d
∫25t6+t4+9dt
e
∫258t5+9t3+6dt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we find r′(t) and ‖r′(t)‖:

r′(t)=ddt(t3)i+ddt(3t)j+ddt(t4)k=3t2i+3j+4t3k‖r′(t)‖=(3t2)2+(3)2+(4t3)2=9t4+9+16t6

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is:

L=∫25‖r′(t)‖dt=∫2516t6+9t4+9dt

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms r′(t)=⟨3t²,3,4t³⟩, giving speed √(16t⁶+9t⁴+9). Its integral from 2 to 5 is option a. The deliberately submitted option b omits the squared middle component, 9.

content.knowledge_point: Finding an Integral Expression For the Arc Length of a Curve
content.problem: Which integral expression gives the arc length of the curve $r(t)={t}^{3}\,i+3t\,j+{t}^{4}\,k$ from  $t=2$ to $t=5?$
content.worked_solution:
First, we find ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{4})\,k \\  & =3{t}^{2}\,i+3\,j+4{t}^{3}\,k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(3{t}^{2})^{2}+(3)^{2}+(4{t}^{3})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9{t}^{4}+9+16{t}^{6}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is:

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{2}^{5}‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t={\int }_{2}^{5}\sqrt{16{t}^{6}+9{t}^{4}+9}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Which integral expression gives the arc length of the curve f(t)=et(i+2j+tk) from t=1 to t=2?

a
∫12ett2+2t+5dt
b
∫01et(t+2)dt
c
∫01ett2+2t+2dt
d
∫12ett2+2t+6dt
e
∫12ett2+2t+4dt
Submit

decision.explanation: By the product rule, f′(t)=e^t⟨1,2,t+1⟩. Its magnitude is e^t√(1+4+(t+1)²)=e^t√(t²+2t+6). Integrating this speed from 1 to 2 gives option d.

Which integral expression gives the arc length of the curve f(t)=et(i+2j+tk) from t=1 to t=2?

a
∫12ett2+2t+5dt

∫01et(t+2)dt
c
∫01ett2+2t+2dt

∫12ett2+2t+6dt
e
∫12ett2+2t+4dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we find f′(t) and ‖f′(t)‖:

f′(t)=ddt(et)i+ddt(2et)j+ddt(tet)k=eti+2etj+(tet+et)k‖f′(t)‖=(et)2+(2et)2+(et(t+1))2=e2t+4e2t+e2t(t2+2t+1)=e2t(1+4+t2+2t+1)=ett2+2t+6

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is

L=∫12‖f′(t)‖dt=∫12ett2+2t+6dt.
